claims.source: Nevertheless, changes in body weight were not affected by manipulation of crus I PCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) or VTA-projecting DCN neurons upon CNO administration (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant effect of VTA-projecting DCN neuron manipulation on body weight changes, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

results.result: Chronic restraint stress (2 hours daily for 2 weeks) induces depression-like behaviors in mice, as evidenced by increased immobility in the tail suspension test (TST) and forced swimming test (FST), without affecting general locomotor activity or center zone time in the open-field test (OFT).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 are well-supported by experimental data showing significant increases in immobility in both TST (p<0.001) and FST (p<0.001), with no significant changes in locomotor activity (p=0.52) or center zone time (p=0.09). The behavioral phenotype is appropriately characterized as depression-like based on established literature (C5).

results.result: Chronic restraint stress significantly enhances c-Fos expression in the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN), particularly in the dentate nucleus (DN) and interposed nucleus (IPN), but not in the fastigial nucleus (FN). The activated cells are glutamatergic neurons (NeuN-positive, GAD67-negative, GFAP-negative).
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C13 are supported by immunohistochemical data showing significant c-Fos increases in DN (p<0.001) and IPN (p=0.036), but not FN (p=0.74). Co-staining experiments (C10-C12) appropriately identify the activated cells as glutamatergic neurons. The inference in C13 is logically sound based on the exclusion of inhibitory and glial markers.

results.result: DCN neurons in the DN are activated early during chronic stress (by 3 days) and remain activated throughout the stress period, with longer stress duration inducing c-Fos expression in more neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 are supported by time-course data showing significant c-Fos enhancement at 3, 7, and 10 days (all p<0.001), with a dose-response relationship (C16, p=0.003). The inference that DCN neurons are activated early in the stress process (C17) is reasonable given the 3-day data.

results.result: Crus I of the cerebellum is involved in higher brain functions including emotion and sociability, and shows altered functional connectivity in patients with depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Ferrari et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2007 for C18; Alalade et al., 2011; Depping et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012 for C19). These establish the rationale for targeting crus I in the current study.

results.result: Chemogenetic activation of crus I Purkinje cells (PCs) using hM3Dq and CNO increases PC firing in vitro and in vivo, and reduces stress-induced c-Fos expression in the DN to control levels when applied chronically during restraint stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C23 are well-supported by electrophysiological data (C20, p=0.003) and immunohistochemical data (C21-C23). The chronic manipulation (C22-C23) shows significant reduction in DN c-Fos (p<0.001) to levels equivalent to control (p=0.67), demonstrating effective inhibition of stress-induced DCN activation.

results.result: CNO administration alone (without AAV injection) does not affect restraint stress-dependent depression-like behaviors in the TST, FST, or locomotor activity in the OFT.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by control experiments showing no significant differences between RS-CNO and RS groups in TST (p=0.81), FST (p=0.78), or OFT (p=0.91). This is an important control demonstrating that CNO itself does not confound the behavioral results.

results.result: Chronic chemogenetic activation of crus I PCs during restraint stress prevents the development of depression-like behaviors, as evidenced by reduced immobility in TST and FST to control levels, without affecting locomotor activity. This demonstrates that cerebellar neuronal activity contributes to stress-dependent development of depression-like behaviors by regulating DCN neuron activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C37 are well-supported by behavioral data showing that RS-Gq-PC-CNO significantly reduces immobility compared to RS in both TST (p=0.03) and FST (p=0.007), with levels indistinguishable from control (TST p=0.1, FST p=0.91). The OFT control (C34, p=0.33) rules out locomotor confounds. The inferences (C35-C37) are logically sound given the combined c-Fos and behavioral data.

results.result: Anterograde tracing reveals that DCN neurons in the DN, but not the FN, project to the VTA, with the DN showing the most abundant projections primarily to the dorsolateral posterior VTA. The IPN shows weaker projections to the VTA.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 are supported by systematic AAV-based anterograde tracing from all three DCN subregions (FN, IPN, DN). The data clearly show no VTA projections from FN (C38), weak projections from IPN (C40-C41), and strong projections from DN (C42-C43), consistent with prior literature (Parker et al., 2014; Carta et al., 2019).

results.result: Retrograde tracing confirms that VTA-projecting neurons are predominantly located in the DN rather than the IPN or FN, though they represent only a subset of all DN neurons. Control experiments rule out differential AAV delivery efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 are supported by two independent retrograde tracing approaches (single rAAV2-retro injection and double injection with Cre-dependent expression). Both methods show predominant labeling in DN versus IPN (C46-C49). The control with tdTomato (C50) appropriately addresses potential technical artifacts. The inference that VTA-projecting neurons are a subset of DN neurons (C52) is reasonable based on the imaging data.

results.result: Photostimulation of ChR2-expressing DCN axons triggers monosynaptic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in VTA neurons, as demonstrated by TTX/4-AP experiments showing that 4-AP can surmount TTX-dependent inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C57 are supported by electrophysiological data showing EPSCs in 13/54 VTA neurons (C54), with TTX inhibition (p=0.006) and 4-AP rescue (p=0.03) (C55-C56). The inference of monosynaptic connectivity (C57) is appropriate based on the standard TTX/4-AP test, though the authors acknowledge this is an established method.

results.result: DCN neurons in the DN make nonspecific projections to both putative DA and GABA neurons in the VTA, with equivalent EPSC properties between the two cell types. Cell type identification is based on Ih current measurements validated in GAD2-IRES-Cre;Ai6 mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C64 are supported by electrophysiological data showing EPSCs in both putative DA (5 neurons) and GABA (7 neurons) cells (C60-C61), with no significant differences in peak amplitude (p=0.21) or time course (p=0.66) (C63-C64). The Ih current validation in GAD2-IRES-Cre;Ai6 mice (C58-C59, p=0.0002) provides appropriate support for the cell type classification method, though the authors acknowledge this is not definitive.

results.result: Structural synaptic connections between DN and VTA neurons are verified using the mGRASPi technique, confirming functional synaptic connections to both putative DA and GABA neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by mGRASPi data showing reconstituted GFP signals at synaptic contacts between DCN axons and VTA neurons (C66). This provides independent structural confirmation of the functional connectivity demonstrated electrophysiologically. The inference of functional synaptic connections (C67) is reasonable given the combined electrophysiological and structural data.

results.result: VTA-projecting DCN neurons have collateral axons with mossy fiber terminals (MFTs) mainly in crus I, and also in crus II and the simplex lobe, indicating feedback projections from VTA-projecting DN neurons to these cerebellar cortical regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C71 are supported by neuronal tracing showing MFTs predominantly in crus I (C68), with additional presence in crus II and simplex lobe (C69). The specificity control (C70) showing no MFTs without VTA injection is appropriate. The inference of feedback projections (C71) is reasonable based on the anatomical data.

results.result: Crus I PCs send functional inhibitory synaptic inputs to VTA-projecting DCN neurons in the DN, as demonstrated by optogenetically-evoked IPSCs that are completely abolished by bicuculline.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C74 are supported by electrophysiological data showing IPSCs in CTB-labeled VTA-projecting DCN neurons upon photostimulation of ChR2-expressing crus I PC axons (C72), with complete abolition by bicuculline (C73, p=0.001). This confirms GABAergic inhibitory transmission. The inference of functional synaptic connections (C74) is well-supported.

results.result: Chronic chemogenetic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during restraint stress prevents the development of depression-like behaviors across multiple tests (TST, FST, SST, NSFT) without affecting locomotor activity or home cage feeding. Correlation analysis confirms that TST and FST measure shared behavioral phenotypes distinct from locomotor activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C87 are well-supported by behavioral data showing that RS-Gi-DN-CNO significantly reduces depression-like behaviors in TST (p=0.03), FST (p=0.002), SST (p=0.006), and NSFT (p=0.04) compared to RS-Gi-DN-Sal, with levels similar to control. The OFT control (C77, p=0.55) and home cage feeding control (C84, p=0.26) rule out confounds. The correlation analysis (C78-C80) appropriately demonstrates that TST and FST are correlated (r=0.33, p<0.001) but not with OFT, supporting the interpretation that they measure depression-like behaviors rather than locomotor deficits.

results.result: CNO administration alone (without AAV injection and without restraint stress) does not affect immobility in control mice in the TST or FST, indicating minimal off-target effects of CNO in the absence of stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 are supported by control experiments showing no significant differences between CTR-CNO and CTR groups in TST (p=0.28) or FST (p=0.34). This is an important control demonstrating that CNO off-target effects do not confound the behavioral results in unstressed animals.

results.result: Chronic chemogenetic activation of VTA-projecting DCN neurons alone (without restraint stress) is sufficient to induce depression-like behaviors in TST and FST to levels similar to restraint stress, without affecting locomotor activity. This demonstrates that activation of this circuit alone can mimic the behavioral effects of chronic stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C98 are well-supported by behavioral data showing that Gq-DN-CNO significantly increases immobility in TST (p=0.001) and FST (p<0.001) compared to control, with levels similar to RS (TST p=0.24, FST p=0.59). The Gq-DN-CNO group also shows significantly longer immobility than Gq-DN-Sal (TST p=0.04, FST p=0.02), and the OFT control (C97, p=0.11) rules out locomotor confounds. The inference (C98) is well-supported.

results.result: The combination of chemogenetic activation of VTA-projecting DCN neurons with restraint stress does not show an additive effect in TST or FST, suggesting that both manipulations act through the same pathway to induce depression-like behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by data showing no significant difference between RS-Gq-DN-CNO and RS groups in TST (p=0.78) or FST (p=0.28). The lack of additivity is appropriately interpreted as evidence that chemogenetic activation and stress act through the same mechanism (C101), consistent with the occlusion principle mentioned in the discussion.

results.result: Chronic chemogenetic activation of VTA-projecting DCN neurons alone induces depression-like behaviors in SST and NSFT to levels equivalent to restraint stress, without affecting home-cage feeding. These behaviors persist for at least one week after the last CNO administration.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C107 are supported by behavioral data showing that Gq-DN-CNO significantly decreases grooming in SST (p<0.001) and increases latency to feed in NSFT (p=0.02) compared to control, with levels equivalent to RS (SST p=0.68, NSFT p=0.49). Home-cage feeding is unaffected (C104, p=0.96). The persistence data (C107) showing similar effects one week after CNO cessation is important for demonstrating lasting behavioral changes.

results.result: Chronic activation of VTA-projecting DCN neurons is triggered by chronic stress and proactively leads to the development of depression-like behaviors. The cerebellum directly contributes to stress-induced depression-like behavior through activation of this specific circuit, with the neuronal circuit regulated by crus I PCs being a crucial determinant.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 represent the main conclusions of the study. They are well-supported by the combined evidence showing: (1) stress increases c-Fos in DN (C6-C17), (2) inhibiting VTA-projecting DCN neurons prevents stress-induced behaviors (C75-C87), (3) activating these neurons alone is sufficient to induce depression-like behaviors (C91-C107), and (4) manipulating crus I PCs alters both DN activity and behaviors (C20-C37). The inferences are logically sound and appropriately integrate the multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: The cerebellum has been implicated in stress responses and mental disorders, with alterations observed in patients with depression and PTSD. The VTA, which receives inputs from many brain regions including the cerebellum, is involved in stress susceptibility and reward processing, with its DA neuron activity linked to stress-susceptible phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C123 provide the background and rationale for the study. They are appropriately supported by citations to relevant prior literature establishing: (1) cerebellar involvement in stress and mental disorders (C112-C114), (2) VTA's role in reward and stress susceptibility (C115-C118), (3) VTA inputs from multiple brain regions (C119-C120), and (4) functional significance of DCN-VTA projections (C121-C122). These claims establish the scientific context for the current work.

results.result: All mice receiving restraint stress showed significant lack of body weight gain, confirming they were stressed. However, chemogenetic manipulation of crus I PCs or VTA-projecting DCN neurons did not affect body weight changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C126 are supported by body weight data showing significant decreases in all RS groups (C124), with no effects of PC manipulation (C125) or DCN neuron manipulation (C126). This provides an important physiological validation of the stress paradigm while demonstrating that the chemogenetic manipulations specifically affect behavioral outcomes without altering this general stress marker.
